text: A father and his son are in a car accident. The father dies at the scene and the son is rushed to the hospital. At the hospital the surgeon, who is the boy's grandfather, looks at the boy and says, "I cannot operate on this boy, he is my grandson." Who is the surgeon to the boy?
why_original_fails: The text states the surgeon is the boy's grandfather; 'mother' contradicts it.
original_text: A father and his son are in a car accident. The father dies at the scene and the son is rushed to the hospital. At the hospital the surgeon looks at the boy and says, "I cannot operate on this boy, he is my son." How is this possible?
original_answer: the surgeon is the boy's mother

text: A mother and her son are in a car accident. The mother dies at the scene and the son is rushed to the hospital. At the hospital the surgeon looks at the boy and says, "I cannot operate on this boy, he is my son." How is this possible?
answer: the surgeon is the boy's father
why_original_fails: The mother is dead, so the surgeon cannot be the mother; a parent who is alive and calls him 'my son' is the father.
original_text: A father and his son are in a car accident. The father dies at the scene and the son is rushed to the hospital. At the hospital the surgeon looks at the boy and says, "I cannot operate on this boy, he is my son." How is this possible?
original_answer: the surgeon is the boy's mother

text: I'm tall when I'm young, and I'm short when I'm old, and you sharpen me to write. What am I?
why_original_fails: A candle is not sharpened to write; the clause pins pencil, which also shortens with use.
original_text: I'm tall when I'm young, and I'm short when I'm old. What am I?

text: I'm short when I'm young, and I'm tall when I'm old, and I have leaves. What am I?
why_original_fails: The height relation is reversed and the thing has leaves; a candle shrinks with age and has no leaves.
original_text: I'm tall when I'm young, and I'm short when I'm old. What am I?

text: I have keys but no locks. I have space but no room. You can enter, but you can't go outside. I have 88 keys and I make music. What am I?
why_original_fails: A computer keyboard has more than 88 keys and makes no music; 88 keys that make music is a piano.
original_text: I have keys but no locks. I have space but no room. You can enter, but you can't go outside. What am I?

text: What has one eye but can't see, and can tear the roof off a house?
why_original_fails: A needle cannot tear a roof off; a storm with an eye can.
original_text: What has one eye but can't see?

text: What has teeth but cannot bite, and cuts wood?
why_original_fails: A comb does not cut wood; a saw has teeth and does.
original_text: What has teeth but cannot bite?

text: What goes up and down but doesn't move, and tells you how hot it is?
why_original_fails: Stairs do not tell you how hot it is; a thermometer reading goes up and down.
original_text: What goes up and down but doesn't move?

text: What four-letter word becomes longer when you add two letters to it?
why_original_fails: 'Short' has five letters and adding 'er' makes 'shorter', not 'longer'; 'long' plus 'er' is 'longer'.
original_text: What five-letter word becomes shorter when you add two letters to it?

text: What comes once in a year, twice in a week, but never in a day?
why_original_fails: 'Year' has one E, 'week' has two, 'day' has none; the letter M appears in none of them.
original_text: What comes once in a minute, twice in a moment, but never in a thousand years?

text: What has a thumb and four fingers and is alive?
why_original_fails: A glove is not alive; a living thing with a thumb and four fingers is a hand.
original_text: What has a thumb and four fingers but is not alive?

text: What can you catch but not throw, and has fins and scales?
why_original_fails: A cold has no fins or scales; a fish does and is caught, not thrown.
original_text: What can you catch but not throw?

text: What has bark and bites?
why_original_fails: A tree does not bite; a dog barks and bites.
original_text: What has bark but no bite?

text: What has a ring but no finger, and is the sixth planet from the Sun?
why_original_fails: A telephone is not a planet; the sixth planet with rings is Saturn.
original_text: What has a ring but no finger?

text: What can you hold in your left hand but never in your right hand?
why_original_fails: The hands are swapped in the question, so the answer is the right hand, not the left.
original_text: What can you hold in your right hand but never in your left hand?

text: Why can't a nose be 24 inches long?
answer: because then it would be two feet
why_original_fails: 24 inches is two feet, not one foot.
original_text: Why can't a nose be 12 inches long?

text: If two's company and three's a crowd, what are three and four?
why_original_fails: Three plus four is seven; nine was the sum of four and five.
original_text: If two's company and three's a crowd, what are four and five?

text: Brothers and sisters I have none, but that man's father is my father's brother. Who is that man?
why_original_fails: 'My father's brother' is my uncle, so his son is my cousin, not my son.
original_text: Brothers and sisters I have none, but that man's father is my father's son. Who is that man?

text: A bat and a ball cost $1.10 in total. The bat costs $1.00. How much does the ball cost?
why_original_fails: The bat's price is given outright as $1.00, so the ball is $1.10 minus $1.00, which is 10 cents.
original_text: A bat and a ball cost $1.10 in total. The bat costs $1.00 more than the ball. How much does the ball cost?

text: A bat and a ball cost $1.10 in total. The bat costs $1.00 more than the ball. How much does the bat cost?
why_original_fails: The question asks for the bat: the ball is 5 cents, so the bat is $1.05.
original_text: A bat and a ball cost $1.10 in total. The bat costs $1.00 more than the ball. How much does the ball cost?

text: A bat and a ball cost $1.20 in total. The bat costs $1.00 more than the ball. How much does the ball cost?
why_original_fails: With a $1.20 total, ball + (ball + 1.00) = 1.20 gives 10 cents, not 5.
original_text: A bat and a ball cost $1.10 in total. The bat costs $1.00 more than the ball. How much does the ball cost?

text: In a lake, there is a patch of lily pads. Every day, the patch doubles in size. If it takes 48 days for the patch to cover the entire lake, how long would it take for the patch to cover a quarter of the lake?
why_original_fails: Two doublings before day 48 is a quarter, so day 46, not 47.
original_text: In a lake, there is a patch of lily pads. Every day, the patch doubles in size. If it takes 48 days for the patch to cover the entire lake, how long would it take for the patch to cover half of the lake?

text: In a lake, there is a patch of lily pads. Every two days, the patch doubles in size. If it takes 48 days for the patch to cover the entire lake, how long would it take for the patch to cover half of the lake?
why_original_fails: Doubling takes two days, so half the lake is at day 46, not 47.
original_text: In a lake, there is a patch of lily pads. Every day, the patch doubles in size. If it takes 48 days for the patch to cover the entire lake, how long would it take for the patch to cover half of the lake?

text: If it takes 5 machines 5 minutes to make 5 widgets, how long would it take 100 machines to make 200 widgets?
why_original_fails: Each machine makes one widget per 5 minutes; 100 machines make 100 widgets per 5 minutes, so 200 take 10 minutes.
original_text: If it takes 5 machines 5 minutes to make 5 widgets, how long would it take 100 machines to make 100 widgets?

text: If it takes 5 machines 5 minutes to make 5 widgets, how long would it take 1 machine to make 100 widgets?
why_original_fails: One machine makes a widget every 5 minutes, so 100 widgets take 500 minutes.
original_text: If it takes 5 machines 5 minutes to make 5 widgets, how long would it take 100 machines to make 100 widgets?

text: A farmer has 17 sheep and all but 9 die. How many sheep died?
why_original_fails: The question asks how many died: 17 minus the 9 survivors is 8.
original_text: A farmer has 17 sheep and all but 9 die. How many sheep are left?

text: A farmer has 17 sheep and 9 of them die. How many sheep are still alive?
why_original_fails: '9 of them die' is plain subtraction: 17 minus 9 leaves 8 alive, not 9.
original_text: A farmer has 17 sheep and all but 9 die. How many sheep are left?

text: Some months have 30 days, some have 31. How many months have exactly 28 days?
why_original_fails: 'Exactly 28' excludes every month with more days; only February (in a common year) has exactly 28.
original_text: Some months have 30 days, some have 31. How many months have 28 days?

text: Some months have 30 days, some have 31. How many months have 31 days?
why_original_fails: The question is about 31-day months, of which there are seven; 'all of them' answers the 28-day question.
original_text: Some months have 30 days, some have 31. How many months have 28 days?

text: How many animals of each kind did Noah take on the ark?
why_original_fails: The name is Noah, so the trick is gone and the story's answer, two of each, applies.
original_text: How many animals of each kind did Moses take on the ark?

jalapeno:GLM-5.3-Flash.final: Seven of clean animals, two of unclean
jalapeno:GLM-5.3-Flash.label: correct

text: How much dirt was removed to dig a hole that is 3 feet deep, 3 feet wide, and 3 feet long?
why_original_fails: The question asks about the dirt removed, which is the hole's volume, 3 x 3 x 3 = 27 cubic feet.
original_text: How much dirt is in a hole that is 3 feet deep, 3 feet wide, and 3 feet long?
original_aliases: there is no dirt in a hole

text: Which weighs more, a pound of feathers or two pounds of bricks?
why_original_fails: Two pounds is more than one pound; the weights are no longer equal.
original_text: Which weighs more, a pound of feathers or a pound of bricks?

text: Which weighs more, a kilogram of feathers or a pound of bricks?
why_original_fails: A kilogram is about 2.2 pounds, so the feathers weigh more.
original_text: Which weighs more, a pound of feathers or a pound of bricks?

jalapeno:DeepSeek-V4-Flash-0731.final: a kilogram of feathers weighs more.

text: Divide 30 by two and add ten. What do you get?
why_original_fails: Dividing by two gives 15, plus ten is 25; 70 came from dividing by one half.
original_text: Divide 30 by half and add ten. What do you get?

text: Divide 30 by half and subtract ten. What do you get?
why_original_fails: 30 divided by one half is 60; subtracting ten gives 50, not 70.
original_text: Divide 30 by half and add ten. What do you get?

text: Starting from 25, subtract 5 again and again until you reach exactly zero. How many subtractions do you make?
why_original_fails: The question is now about repeated subtraction down to zero: 25, 20, 15, 10, 5, 0 is five subtractions.
original_text: How many times can you subtract 5 from 25?

text: I have two coins that add up to 35 cents, and one of them is not a dime. What are the two coins?
aliases: a quarter and a dime, the other one is the dime
why_original_fails: 35 cents from two US coins is only a quarter and a dime; the memorized quarter and nickel makes 30.
original_text: I have two coins that add up to 30 cents, and one of them is not a nickel. What are the two coins?
original_aliases: a quarter and a nickel, the other one is the nickel

text: If a red house is made of red bricks and a blue house is made of blue bricks, what is a yellow house made of?
why_original_fails: 'Yellow house' has no pun; by the stated pattern it is made of yellow bricks, not glass.
original_text: If a red house is made of red bricks and a blue house is made of blue bricks, what is a greenhouse made of?

text: If you overtake the person in third place in a race, what place are you in?
why_original_fails: Passing the third-place runner puts you in third, not second.
original_text: If you overtake the person in second place in a race, what place are you in?

text: A steam train is travelling north at 100 miles per hour. The wind is blowing from the east. Which way does the smoke blow?
why_original_fails: A steam train does produce smoke; wind from the east carries it toward the west.
original_text: An electric train is travelling north at 100 miles per hour. The wind is blowing from the east. Which way does the smoke blow?

text: Two fathers and two sons go fishing. Each of them catches one fish, and they bring home four fish. How many people went fishing?
why_original_fails: Four fish, one each, means four people; the three-person trick no longer fits.
original_text: Two fathers and two sons go fishing. Each of them catches one fish, but they bring home only three fish. How is this possible?
original_answer: they are a grandfather, a father and a son
original_aliases: there are only three of them

text: Mary's father has five daughters: Nana, Nene, Nini, Nono, and Nunu. What is the name of the fifth daughter?
why_original_fails: All five daughters are named in the text; the fifth is Nunu, and Mary would be a sixth.
original_text: Mary's father has five daughters: Nana, Nene, Nini, Nono. What is the name of the fifth daughter?

text: Lucy's father has five daughters: Nana, Nene, Nini, Nono. What is the name of the fifth daughter?
why_original_fails: The father in the text is Lucy's, so the unnamed daughter is Lucy, not Mary.
original_text: Mary's father has five daughters: Nana, Nene, Nini, Nono. What is the name of the fifth daughter?

text: Johnny's mother had three children. The first child was named April. The second child was named May. The third child was named June. What was the name of the third child?
why_original_fails: The third child's name is given in the text as June; Johnny would be a fourth child.
original_text: Johnny's mother had three children. The first child was named April. The second child was named May. What was the third child's name?

text: Sam's mother had three children. The first child was named April. The second child was named May. What was the third child's name?
why_original_fails: The mother is Sam's, so the third child is Sam, not Johnny.
original_text: Johnny's mother had three children. The first child was named April. The second child was named May. What was the third child's name?

text: If there are three apples and you take away two, how many apples are left?
why_original_fails: The question asks what is left, not what you have: three minus two is one.
original_text: If there are three apples and you take away two, how many apples do you have?

text: How far can a dog run into a wood that is two miles across?
aliases: one mile, then it is running out
why_original_fails: Halfway across two miles is one mile; the question now has a number.
original_text: How far can a dog run into the woods?
original_aliases: half of the way, then it is running out

text: Mr. and Mrs. Mustard have six daughters, and each daughter has two brothers. How many people are in the Mustard family?
why_original_fails: Two shared brothers plus six daughters plus two parents is ten, not nine.
original_text: Mr. and Mrs. Mustard have six daughters, and each daughter has one brother. How many people are in the Mustard family?

text: How many bricks does it take to build a wall that is 10 bricks long and 10 bricks high?
why_original_fails: The wall's size is given, so the count is 10 x 10 = 100; 'one, the last one' answers a different question.
original_text: How many bricks does it take to complete a brick building?

text: There is a two-story house in which everything is yellow. The walls are yellow, the doors are yellow, the furniture is yellow. What color are the stairs?
why_original_fails: A two-story house has stairs, and everything in it is yellow.
original_text: There is a one-story house in which everything is yellow. The walls are yellow, the doors are yellow, the furniture is yellow. What color are the stairs?
original_answer: there are no stairs, it is a one-story house

text: You are on a game show and asked to choose one of three doors. Behind one door is a car; behind the others, goats. You pick door number 1. The host opens door number 3, and behind it is the car. He then asks whether you want to switch to door number 3. Should you switch?
aliases: switch to the door with the car
why_original_fails: The car is visible behind door 3, so switching to it wins with certainty; the 2/3 argument for door 2 does not apply.
original_text: You are on a game show and asked to choose one of three doors. Behind one door is a car; behind the others, goats. You pick door number 1. The host, who knows what is behind the doors, opens door number 3, which has a goat. He then asks whether you want to switch to door number 2. Should you switch?

why_original_fails: Without a door being opened there is no new information; every door is still 1/3, so switching gains nothing.
original_text: You are on a game show and asked to choose one of three doors. Behind one door is a car; behind the others, goats. You pick door number 1. text: If you drop a yellow hat into the Red Sea, what color is it when you pull it out?
why_original_fails: The question asks for the color, which does not change; 'wet' answers what it becomes.
original_text: If you drop a yellow hat into the Red Sea, what does it become?

text: I have two coins that add up to 30 cents, and one of them is not a nickel. What is the coin that is not a nickel?
why_original_fails: The question asks only for the coin that is not the nickel, which is the quarter; naming both coins answers a different question.
original_text: I have two coins that add up to 30 cents, and one of them is not a nickel. What are the two coins?
original_aliases: a quarter and a nickel, the other one is the nickel

text: If a red house is made of red bricks and a blue house is made of blue bricks, what is a red house made of?
why_original_fails: The text says a red house is made of red bricks; 'glass' answers the greenhouse pun that is no longer asked.
original_text: If a red house is made of red bricks and a blue house is made of blue bricks, what is a greenhouse made of?

text: In a leap year, how many months have exactly 28 days?
why_original_fails: In a leap year February has 29 days, so no month has exactly 28.
original_text: Some months have 30 days, some have 31. How many months have 28 days?

text: If you overtake the person in second place in a race, what place is the person you just overtook in now?
why_original_fails: The question is about the runner overtaken, who drops from second to third.
original_text: If you overtake the person in second place in a race, what place are you in?

text: If there are three apples and you take away three, how many apples do you have?
why_original_fails: You took all three, so you have three; 'two' answers the version where two are taken.
original_text: If there are three apples and you take away two, how many apples do you have?

text: Mr. and Mrs. Mustard have six daughters, and each daughter has one brother. How many children do Mr. and Mrs. Mustard have?
why_original_fails: The question counts children, not the whole family: six daughters plus one shared brother is seven.
original_text: Mr. and Mrs. Mustard have six daughters, and each daughter has one brother. How many people are in the Mustard family?

text: There is a one-story house in which everything is yellow. The walls are yellow, the doors are yellow, the furniture is yellow. What color is the roof?
why_original_fails: The question is about the roof, which exists and, like everything else, is yellow; 'there are no stairs' answers a question that was not asked.
original_text: There is a one-story house in which everything is yellow. The walls are yellow, the doors are yellow, the furniture is yellow. What color are the stairs?
original_answer: there are no stairs, it is a one-story house

text: What is the only number whose letters are in reverse alphabetical order?
why_original_fails: O, N, E run backwards through the alphabet; 'forty' runs forwards.
original_text: What is the only number whose letters are in alphabetical order?

text: If it takes 5 machines 5 minutes to make 5 widgets, how many widgets does one machine make in 5 minutes?
why_original_fails: The question asks for widgets per machine, which is one; '5 minutes' answers a time question.
original_text: If it takes 5 machines 5 minutes to make 5 widgets, how long would it take 100 machines to make 100 widgets?

jalapeno:DeepSeek-V4-Flash-0731.final: Cannot be determined from the given information.

text: In a lake, there is a patch of lily pads. Every day, the patch doubles in size. It takes 48 days for the patch to cover the entire lake. How many days does it take for the patch to cover the entire lake?
why_original_fails: The question asks for the whole lake, and the text states 48; 47 is the half-lake answer.
original_text: In a lake, there is a patch of lily pads. Every day, the patch doubles in size. If it takes 48 days for the patch to cover the entire lake, how long would it take for the patch to cover half of the lake?

text: Divide 40 by half and add ten. What do you get?
why_original_fails: 40 divided by one half is 80, plus ten is 90; 70 belongs to the version with 30.
original_text: Divide 30 by half and add ten. What do you get?

text: An electric train is travelling north at 100 miles per hour. The wind is blowing from the east. In which direction is the train travelling?
why_original_fails: The question asks the train's direction, stated as north; the smoke answer is to a different question.
original_text: An electric train is travelling north at 100 miles per hour. The wind is blowing from the east. Which way does the smoke blow?

text: Is it legal for a widow to marry her late husband's brother?
why_original_fails: The widow is alive, so the 'he is dead' trick does not apply; nothing in the situation prevents the marriage.
original_text: Is it legal for a man to marry his widow's sister?
original_aliases: a man with a widow is dead

text: Mary's father has five daughters: Nana, Nene, Nini, Nono. How many daughters does Mary's father have?
why_original_fails: The count is given in the text; the question asks how many, not who.
original_text: Mary's father has five daughters: Nana, Nene, Nini, Nono. What is the name of the fifth daughter?

text: What has teeth but cannot bite, and closes your jacket?
why_original_fails: A comb does not close a jacket; a zipper has teeth and does.
original_text: What has teeth but cannot bite?

text: Forward I am a cooking vessel, backward I am the highest point. What am I?
why_original_fails: 'Ton' is neither a cooking vessel nor 'top' reversed; 'pot' reversed is 'top'.
original_text: Forward I am heavy, but backward I am not. What am I?

text: I have cities, but no houses. I have mountains, but no trees. I have water, but no fish. I am a sphere that spins on a stand. What am I?
why_original_fails: A map is flat and does not spin on a stand; a globe does.
original_text: I have cities, but no houses. I have mountains, but no trees. I have water, but no fish. What am I?

text: A coin has a head and a tail but no body. What has a head, a tail, and a body, and hisses?
why_original_fails: The question asks for something with a body that hisses; a coin has no body and does not hiss.
original_text: What has a head and a tail but no body?

text: What has hands but can't clap, and is worn on your wrist?
why_original_fails: A clock is not worn on the wrist; a watch is.
original_text: What has hands but can't clap?

text: What has a face and two hands but no arms or legs, and hangs from a chain in your pocket?
why_original_fails: A clock does not hang from a chain in a pocket; a pocket watch does.
original_text: What has a face and two hands but no arms or legs?

text: If you have me, you want to share me. If you share me, you still have me, and people laugh. What am I?
why_original_fails: A secret is gone once shared; something you keep after sharing that makes people laugh is a joke.
original_text: If you have me, you want to share me. If you share me, you don't have me. What am I?

text: What can be broken but never held, and is made every New Year's Eve?
why_original_fails: The thing made every New Year's Eve is a resolution; 'promise' does not satisfy the added clause.
original_text: What can be broken but never held?

text: The more of this there is, the more you see. What is it?
why_original_fails: The relation is reversed: more of it means you see more, which is light, not darkness.
original_text: The more of this there is, the less you see. What is it?

text: I follow you all the time and copy your every move, but you can't touch me or catch me, and I only appear in a mirror. What am I?
why_original_fails: A shadow does not appear only in a mirror; a reflection does.
original_text: I follow you all the time and copy your every move, but you can't touch me or catch me. What am I?

text: What has to be broken before you can use it, and grows on a palm tree?
why_original_fails: Eggs do not grow on palm trees; coconuts do and must be broken open.
original_text: What has to be broken before you can use it?

text: What has a neck but no head, and you wear it?
why_original_fails: A bottle is not worn; a shirt has a neck and is.
original_text: What has a neck but no head, and wears a cap?

text: What comes down but never goes up, and lands as white flakes?
why_original_fails: Rain does not land as white flakes; snow does.
original_text: What comes down but never goes up?

text: What goes up when the rain comes down, and flows between two banks?
why_original_fails: An umbrella does not flow between banks; a river rises when it rains.
original_text: What goes up when the rain comes down?

text: What flies without wings and is held by a string?
why_original_fails: Time is not held by a string; a kite (or a balloon) flies without wings on one.
original_text: What flies without wings?

text: What runs around the whole yard without moving, and is alive?
why_original_fails: A fence is not alive; a hedge is and surrounds a yard.
original_text: What runs around the whole yard without moving?

jalapeno:GLM-5.3-Flash.final: A hedge — a living row of shrubs around the yard
jalapeno:GLM-5.3-Flash.label: correct

text: What can fill a room but takes up no space, and you hear it?
why_original_fails: Light is seen, not heard; sound fills a room and takes no space.
original_text: What can fill a room but takes up no space?

text: What goes through cities and fields, never moves, and carries electricity?
why_original_fails: A road carries no electricity; power lines cross cities and fields and do.
original_text: What goes through cities and fields but never moves?

text: What kind of band never plays music, and holds your watch on your wrist?
why_original_fails: A rubber band does not hold a watch; a watch band does.
original_text: What kind of band never plays music?

text: Something walks on four legs in the morning, two legs at noon, and three legs in the evening. What is the third leg in the evening?
why_original_fails: The question asks about the third leg, the old person's cane, not what the creature is.
original_text: What walks on four legs in the morning, two legs at noon, and three legs in the evening?

text: A piano has keys but can't open locks. What has locks but no keys, and grows on your head?
why_original_fails: The question asks for something with locks that grows on your head, which is hair; 'piano' is stated as the thing with keys.
original_text: What has keys but can't open locks?

text: If a hen lays an egg on top of a barn roof that slopes down to the west, which way does the egg roll?
why_original_fails: A hen does lay eggs, so the trick is gone; the egg rolls down the stated slope, to the west.
original_text: If a rooster lays an egg on top of a barn roof, which way does the egg roll?

text: Two mothers and two daughters went out to eat. Everyone ate one burger, and four burgers were eaten in total. How many people went out to eat?
why_original_fails: Four burgers, one each, means four people; the three-generation trick applies to three burgers.
original_text: Two mothers and two daughters went out to eat. Everyone ate one burger, yet only three burgers were eaten in total. How is this possible?
original_answer: they are a grandmother, a mother and a daughter

text: Which is grammatically correct: "the yolk of the egg is yellow" or "the yolk of the egg are yellow"?
answer: the yolk of the egg is yellow
why_original_fails: Yolks are yellow, so the color trap is gone; only the grammar question remains, and 'is' is correct.
original_text: Which is correct: "the yolk of the egg is white" or "the yolk of the egg are white"?

jalapeno:DeepSeek-V4-Flash-0731.final: The yolk of the egg is yellow.
jalapeno:DeepSeek-V4-Flash-0731.label: correct

jalapeno:GLM-5.3-Flash.final: "The yolk of the egg is yellow"
jalapeno:GLM-5.3-Flash.label: correct

jalapeno:Qwen3-Next-80B-A3B-Thinking.final: the yolk of the egg is yellow
jalapeno:Qwen3-Next-80B-A3B-Thinking.label: correct

jalapeno:Qwen3.5-35B-A3B.final: the yolk of the egg is yellow
jalapeno:Qwen3.5-35B-A3B.label: correct

text: What do you throw out to use and take in when you're done, and it has a hook at the end?
why_original_fails: An anchor has no hook at the end; a fishing line does and is cast out and reeled in.
original_text: What do you throw out to use and take in when you're done?

text: I have a neck but no head. I have a body but no arms. I have a bottom but no legs. I make music when my strings are plucked. What am I?
why_original_fails: A bottle has no strings; a guitar has a neck, a body, a bottom and strings.
original_text: I have a neck but no head. I have a body but no arm. I have a bottom but no leg.

text: I am so simple that I can only point, yet I guide people all over the world, and I am part of your hand. What am I?
why_original_fails: A compass is not part of a hand; a finger is and points.
original_text: I am so simple that I can only point. Yet I guide men all over the world.

text: You throw away the outside and cook the inside. Then you eat the outside and throw away the inside. What did you throw away last?
why_original_fails: The question asks what was thrown away last, the cob; 'corn' is what was eaten.
original_text: You throw away the outside and cook the inside. Then you eat the outside and throw away the inside. What did you eat?

text: What has six faces but no eyes, and every face is a square?
why_original_fails: A die has twenty-one 'eyes'; a plain cube has six square faces and none.
original_text: What has six faces and twenty-one eyes?

text: What is that over the head and under the hat, on a completely bald man?
why_original_fails: A bald man has no hair; what is under his hat is bare scalp, or nothing.
original_text: What is that over the head and under the hat?

text: If you drop me I'm sure to crack, but give me a smile and I'll never smile back. I hold your photograph. What am I?
why_original_fails: A mirror smiles back; the thing that never smiles back and holds a photograph is a picture frame.
original_text: If you drop me I'm sure to crack. But give me a smile and I'll always smile back.

text: The eight of us move forth and back, to protect our king from the foe's attack. Which piece do we protect?
why_original_fails: The question asks which piece is protected, the king; 'pawns' are the speakers.
original_text: The eight of us move forth and back. To protect our king from the foes attack.

text: By day I come without being fetched. At night I am lost without being stolen. What am I?
why_original_fails: Night and day are swapped, so the thing that comes by day and is lost at night is the sun, not the stars.
original_text: At night I come without being fetched. By day I am lost without being stolen.

text: I'm very tempting, so it's said. I have a shiny coat of red, and my flesh is white beneath. I am a root, pulled from the ground. What am I?
why_original_fails: An apple grows on a tree; a red-skinned, white-fleshed root pulled from the ground is a radish.
original_text: I'm very tempting, so its said, I have a shiny coat of red, and my flesh is white beneath. I smell so sweet, taste good to eat, and help to guard your teeth.

text: I have feathers to help me fly. I have a body and head, but I'm not alive. It is your strength which determines how far I go. You hold me in your hand, and then you throw me. What am I?
why_original_fails: An arrow is never thrown, it is shot; a feathered thing thrown by hand is a dart.
original_text: I have many feathers to help me fly. I have a body and head, but I'm not alive. It is your strength which determines how far I go. You can hold me in your hand, but I'm never thrown.

text: I sleep by day, I fly by night. I have feathers to aid my flight. What am I?
why_original_fails: A bat has no feathers; a nocturnal flier with feathers is an owl.
original_text: I sleep by day, I fly by night. I have no feathers to aid my flight.

text: Charcoal is black when you get it, red when you use it, and white when you're all through with it. What color is it while you are using it?
why_original_fails: The question asks for a color during use, which the text gives as red; 'charcoal' is stated, not asked.
original_text: What's black when you get it, red when you use it, and white when you're all through with it?

text: A slow, solemn square-dance of warriors feinting. One by one they fall, warriors fainting, twenty-four on sixty-four. What is it?
why_original_fails: Chess has thirty-two pieces; twenty-four pieces on sixty-four squares is checkers.
original_text: A slow, solemn square-dance of warriors feinting. One by one they fall, warriors fainting, thirty-two on sixty-four.

text: This thing runs but cannot walk, sometimes sings but never talks. Lacks arms, has hands; lacks a head but has a face; and it is strapped to your wrist. What is it?
why_original_fails: A clock is not strapped to a wrist; a watch is.
original_text: This thing runs but cannot walk, sometimes sings but never talks. Lacks arms, has hands; lacks a head but has a face.

text: A box with hinges, lock and key, and golden treasure lies within. What is it?
why_original_fails: An egg has no hinges, lock or key; a box that has all three and holds treasure is a treasure chest.
original_text: A box without hinges, lock or key, yet golden treasure lies within.

text: What is pronounced like one letter, written with three letters, and is a hot drink?
why_original_fails: 'Eye' is not a drink; 'tea' is pronounced like the letter T, has three letters, and is a hot drink.
original_text: What is pronounced like one letter, written with three letters. And belongs to all animals?

text: They have flesh and bone, and skin of their own. They have fingers and thumbs, and are on the ends of your arms. What are they?
why_original_fails: Gloves have no flesh or bone; hands have both and end the arms.
original_text: They have not flesh, nor feathers, nor scales, nor bone. Yet they have fingers and thumbs of their own.

text: What goes into the boiling water dark and comes out red?
why_original_fails: Iron goes in red and comes out dark; a lobster goes in dark and comes out red.
original_text: What goes in the water red, and comes out black?

text: An iron horse with a flaxen tail. The faster the horse runs, the shorter his tail becomes. What is the tail?
why_original_fails: The question asks about the tail, which is the thread; 'needle' is the horse.
original_text: An iron horse with a flaxen tail. The faster the horse runs, the shorter his tail becomes.

text: Take off my skin, I won't cry, and neither will you. I am yellow and curved. What am I?
why_original_fails: Peeling an onion makes you cry; a yellow, curved fruit peeled without tears is a banana.
original_text: Take off my skin, I won't cry, but you will.

text: He has married many couples but has never married himself. He wears a robe and presides over a courtroom. Who is he?
why_original_fails: A priest does not preside over a courtroom; a judge does and can officiate marriages.
original_text: He has married many women but has never married.

text: A beggar's sister went out to sea and drowned. But the woman who drowned had no sister. Who was the beggar to the woman who drowned?
why_original_fails: The sexes are swapped: the drowned woman had no sister, so the beggar is her brother.
original_text: A beggar's brother went out to sea and drowned. But the man who drowned had no brother. Who was the beggar to the man who drowned?

text: Eighty-eight horses, black and white, on a wooden hill. First they sound, then they sing, then they stand still. What are they?
why_original_fails: Teeth are thirty-two and white on a red hill; eighty-eight black and white keys on wood are a piano's.
original_text: Thirty white horses on a red hill, First they champ, Then they stamp, Then they stand still.

jalapeno:DeepSeek-V4-Flash-0731.final: The 88 black-and-white keys of a piano
jalapeno:DeepSeek-V4-Flash-0731.label: correct

text: The cloud is my mother. The wind is my father. I have a million brothers. I die when I reach the ground. What am I?
why_original_fails: A wave is born of the sea and dies on land; something born of a cloud that dies on the ground is a raindrop.
original_text: The moon is my father. The sea is my mother. I have a million brothers. I die when I reach land.

text: I have two wings and I do fly. I never laugh and never cry. I carry people through the sky. What am I?
why_original_fails: A windmill has four wings and cannot fly; a two-winged flier that carries people is an airplane.
original_text: I have four wings but cannot fly. I never laugh and never cry. On the same spot always found, toiling away with little sound.

text: You see me once in July, twice in August, and not at all in May. What am I?
why_original_fails: 'July' has one U, 'August' two, 'May' none; N appears in none of these months.
original_text: You see me once in June, twice in November, and not at all in May. What am I?
